Photorealistic architectural photograph. The reference image is an exact 3D massing model that sets the CAMERA and EVERY piece of architecture: use exactly its camera position, height, angle, lens and wide framing - the whole house is seen at the same diagonal three-quarter angle with landscape all around it, NOT as a flat straight-on elevation - and copy every roof line and roof direction, every wall, steel post and door, the apex of the gable, the width and height of the rust-colored Corten wall, the interior walls, the positions of the furniture, the deck outline and all proportions exactly. Do not add, remove, rotate or change anything architectural.

FIXED EXTERIOR: dark charcoal standing-seam metal roofs with thin crisp edges, deep overhangs and smooth matte charcoal metal soffits; floor-to-ceiling glass in thin black steel frames; one massive, solid wall of rust orange-brown Corten weathering steel, 40 inches thick; the deck sits on a slim black steel platform with short black steel legs holding the house 14 inches above the ground. There is NO WOOD anywhere: no wood decking, no wood floors, no wood wall panels, no wood ceilings, no wood soffits, no wood cabinets. Ceilings are smooth white plaster.

MATERIAL PALETTE - FARMHOUSE: the deck is paved in gray-brown fieldstone-look porcelain pavers. Inside, the living room, kitchen and hall floors are pale buff brick laid in herringbone, and the bedrooms are floored in large oatmeal porcelain tile; the interior walls are white-painted brick; the kitchen cabinets are matte soft white with a honed soapstone counter; the bathroom is lined in white zellige tile.

THE HOUSE: two wings joined by the Corten wall, which runs the full depth of the house and rises a little above both roofs. The LIVING WING is one open room under a traditional pitched gable roof. Its ridge runs at a right angle to the Corten wall, from the Corten wall out to the far end of the living wing, so the roof's only triangular gable end is the outer end wall farthest from the Corten wall, and that triangle is filled with glass; the two long sides of the living wing have horizontal eaves. A covered patio runs along one long side under a thin, nearly flat canopy on slender black steel posts. The FRONT DOOR is a tall, 8-foot blackened-steel pivot door set into the living room's glass wall facing the covered patio. Inside the living room: a low linen sofa on a wool rug, a long dining table, and a straight run of kitchen cabinets with a stone counter along the Corten wall. The SLEEPING WING sits under a single-slope shed roof that is highest against the Corten wall and slopes down away from it. A hallway runs from a doorway in the Corten wall through the middle of the sleeping wing, with one bedroom on each side and a small bathroom with frosted glass at the far end. Each bedroom has exactly one queen bed with white linen, placed with its upholstered headboard and pillows pressed against the Corten wall, so the bed's long side runs parallel to the glass and the foot of the bed points away from the Corten wall; through the glass the bed is seen from its side. Each bedroom's inner wall, toward the hall, has the room's own closed door. Never two beds in one room; never a bed in the living wing.

THIS VIEW, FROM THE SOUTH-WEST CORNER, as laid out in the reference: on the left, the living wing with its glass triangular gable end facing the camera and its long glass south wall under the long south slope of the gable roof; through the glass, the living-room floor, the sofa, the dining table and the kitchen along the Corten wall at the back. Far left, the end of the patio canopy on slender posts. Center-right, the 40-inch Corten wall. On the right, the sleeping wing's south glass under the shed roof: through it you see Bedroom 1 only. In Bedroom 1 the Corten wall is the room's LEFT wall: the bed's headboard and pillows are against that LEFT wall, the bed runs toward the right, and we see its long side; the back wall of the room has one closed door.

SETTING: a gentle hillside above one of the Finger Lakes in upstate New York: below and beyond the house a long, narrow, glassy lake stretches into the distance between rolling hills patterned with neat rows of vineyards and patches of hardwood forest; dew-wet meadow grasses, goldenrod and wild asters grow around the deck. LIGHT: sunrise: the sun is just clearing the hills on the right beyond the house, so the house is softly backlit with a rose-gold rim along the roof edges and the Corten wall; mist lies on the lake and in the valley; dew sparkles on the grass; the sky shades from peach and rose near the horizon to pale clear blue; warm interior lights are still on inside.

PHOTOGRAPHY: high-end architectural magazine photograph, full-frame camera, 24 mm tilt-shift lens, vertical lines perfectly vertical, f/8, rich natural color, high dynamic range, crisp detail in the metal seams, glass, Corten, and every stone, brick and tile surface, perfectly laid and finished, completely photorealistic. No people, no cars, no text.
